I have farmed these fields in Quzhou County for more than fifty years. I am seventy-three now, and I do not chase new fads. I know every plot of my land, and I know what the North China Plain gives us: flat ground, decent soil, and not enough rain. That is why I stick to the double-cropping system my father used and his father before him. 

This year, I will plant winter wheat on my six mu after the National Day holiday in October. I will run the rotary tiller through the fields to break up the stubble and level the ground, then sow the improved wheat seeds I buy from the county supply store. These varieties resist lodging and give steady yields. The wheat needs four irrigations—one before winter if the autumn is dry, one when it greens up in spring, one at the jointing stage, and one when the heads are filling—because groundwater is the only way to guarantee a crop here. I will fertilize generously: about twenty jin of nitrogen equivalent per mu, plus phosphate and potash, split between the base dressing and the spring top-dress. I will spray pesticides three times when I see aphids or when the mildew starts.

Come early June, when the wheat grain is hard and golden, I will harvest it immediately. The same day, I will plant summer maize on those same six mu. At my age, I do not have the strength to plough again, and there is no time anyway before the frost comes, so I will plant with no-tillage into the wheat stubble. I use hybrid maize seed. It is expensive, but the yield gain pays for itself. The maize needs three good irrigations—at seedling, at the big trumpet stage, and during grain filling—and two rounds of pesticide, mainly for borer and weeds. I expect about 450 kilograms per mu of wheat and 500 kilograms per mu of maize. That fills my grain bins, feeds my household, and leaves enough to sell for cash.
